result:
There is a light on in an empty house.

Not metaphorically. I mean somewhere, right now, in a town you will never visit, on a street with a name you will never learn, there is a house where no one lives and a light was left on. Maybe in a bathroom. A small, yellowish light that has been on for months. Maybe years.

Someone meant to turn it off. Someone was packing boxes or carrying out a mattress, and they flipped it on because the hallway was dark, and then they forgot. They closed the front door with their hands full and drove away and never came back. And the bulb just stayed on.

It outlasted the argument about who would keep the couch. It outlasted the sale of the house that fell through. It will probably outlast the bulb itself, until one day the filament gives up with a quiet *pop* no one will hear.

I've been thinking about that light a lot lately.

We like to think that important things are big and loud. Wars and weddings and rockets leaving the earth. But most of life is not. Most of life is that light. A small, warm thing burning pointlessly in an empty room, waiting to be noticed.

I think about time like that now. Not as a line, but as a house.

When I was younger, time was a road. You could see where you were going. There were markers. Ten years old, you learn fractions. Sixteen, you get to drive. Eighteen, you leave. You could stand on the road and look forward and think, "in five years I'll be there," and you believed it, because the road looked straight.

Nobody tells you that the road ends and the house begins.

Around some age - twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, it's different for everyone - you stop traveling forward and start walking in circles inside something you've built without realizing. Your habits are the walls. Your job is one room. Your relationship is another. Your body is the floor that creaks in the same place every morning. And you walk from room to room, turning lights on and off, thinking you're still on a road.

But you're home. You're already there.

And like any house, it collects things. Mugs with chipped handles you won't throw away. Half-read books. A drawer full of cables that belong to nothing you own anymore. And memories, which are the worst clutter of all, because you can't put them in the trash.

Do you remember being seven years old on a summer afternoon when it was too hot to go outside? The air conditioner humming. The carpet burning your knees. The way dust looked floating in the sun coming through the blinds? You haven't thought about that in twenty years, and then for no reason you're on the train and it comes back whole. Not as a thought, but as a temperature. You can feel the carpet again.

Why does the brain keep that? What evolutionary purpose does it serve to remember the exact pattern of dust at age seven?

Maybe none. Maybe the brain is not a computer designed for efficiency. Maybe it's a house too, and it just never throws anything away in case you need it later.

We are all hoarders of moments that meant nothing at the time.

I went for a walk last night at 2 a.m. I couldn't sleep. You know that kind of sleeplessness that isn't tiredness, but a buzzing? Like your blood has static in it. I walked through my neighborhood and everyone else was asleep. Every house was dark except for the blue flicker of a television left on, or a porch light. The world felt paused.

And I realized: this is the truest version of the world. Not the daytime world with traffic and emails and people performing being people. The nighttime world where nothing is happening and no one is watching. The planet just breathing.

A dog barked somewhere far away and stopped, as if embarrassed. A cat watched me from a driveway and didn't move. The air smelled like cut grass and cold.

I stood under a streetlight and listened to the hum it makes. That electric buzz that means it's working. I've heard that sound a thousand times and never really heard it. It occurred to me that when I die, that hum will still be there. That streetlight will still buzz for someone else standing under it at 2 a.m., feeling weird about being alive.

And that should be depressing, but it wasn't. It was comforting. Like being part of a relay race where you finally get to put the baton down.

We spend so much energy trying to be significant. To be remembered, to be loved loudly, to leave a mark. Build a company, write a book, have children who look like you. I want those things too. I want to be more than a light left on in an empty house.

But maybe significance is the wrong metric. Maybe instead of trying to be huge, we should try to be warm.

That light in the empty house isn't important. No one needs it. It doesn't illuminate anything useful. It's just warm. It's just proof that someone was there, and that they meant to come back, even if they didn't.

Maybe that's enough for a life. To be a small, warm proof that you were here.

If you can be that - if one person, on a bad day, remembers your laugh the way you remember dust in the sun at age seven - then you have not been pointless. You have been a porch light for someone else.

So I keep thinking about what I'd say if I had a thousand words to use however I wanted. No assignment. No audience to impress. Just a thousand little bricks to build something with.

I would not use them to be clever. I would not use them to argue.

I would use them to say this:

If you are reading this at night and feeling alone, you aren't. There are thousands of us awake right now, buzzing quietly in our houses. We are all standing under different streetlights listening to the same hum.

If you are waiting for your life to start, it's already started. This is it. The waiting *is* the house.

If you have an empty room inside you that you don't know what to do with, leave a light on in it. Not for anyone else. Just so you can find it again later.

And if you can, tomorrow, be kind in a small, strange way. Not a big performance of kindness. Just turn off a light someone else left on. Or leave one on for them.

We're all just walking from room to room here. We might as well make it less dark for each other.
